items.stem: The above excerpts support which one of the following generalizations?
items.stimulus: Source 1: “He who is by nature not his own but another’s man, is by nature a slave; and he may be said to be another’s man who, being a human being, is also a possession.” Source: Aristotle, Politics, Book I (c. 350 BCE; Benjamin Jowett translation, 1885 — public domain). Source 2: Paraphrased from Mary Ann Glendon, “The Forgotten Crucible: The Latin American Influence on the Universal Human Rights Idea” (2003). Glendon argues that as Latin American nations gained independence in the nineteenth century, two intellectual strains merged with an older, more universalist natural-law tradition to produce a distinctively Latin American discourse of rights. She traces its roots to the Spanish Dominicans — above all Bartolomé de Las Casas, the sixteenth-century bishop who condemned slavery and defended Native peoples on the basis of a natural right to liberty grounded in a single common humanity: “All the peoples of the world are humans,” Las Casas wrote, “and all the races of humankind are one.” Following Paolo Carozza and Brian Tierney, Glendon credits Las Casas and his fellow Dominicans with laying the groundwork for a doctrine of natural rights independent of religious revelation, drawn instead from human rationality and free will and from Aristotelian philosophy.
options: After European and Latin American populations interacted economically, most Europeans were more compassionate toward the interests of non-white people.
There was some degree of debate by Spanish explorers over how to treat natives in the New World.
The appeal to natural rights and natural law succeeded in abolishing slavery in the New World.
The European belief in white superiority was used to justify the doctrine of natural rights.
items.explanation: Correct: (B). Source 1 states Aristotle’s “natural slave” doctrine — that some people are by nature suited to be ruled — which Spanish thinkers drew on to justify the subjugation of Native peoples. Source 2 traces the opposing tradition: Las Casas and the Spanish Dominicans argued for a natural right to liberty grounded in a common humanity, a tradition Glendon credits with shaping later human-rights thought. The two excerpts therefore document a genuine debate over how Native peoples should be treated, which is exactly what (B) says — rule out (A). Neither source says anything about abolishing slavery, so rule out (C). And the natural-rights doctrine in the second excerpt was used to challenge, not justify, claims of white superiority, so rule out (D).

items.stem: Which one of the following statements about the Spanish conquest of the Americas is most accurate?
items.stimulus: Source 1: “He who is by nature not his own but another’s man, is by nature a slave; and he may be said to be another’s man who, being a human being, is also a possession.” Source: Aristotle, Politics, Book I (c. 350 BCE; Benjamin Jowett translation, 1885 — public domain). Source 2: Paraphrased from Mary Ann Glendon, “The Forgotten Crucible: The Latin American Influence on the Universal Human Rights Idea” (2003). Glendon argues that as Latin American nations gained independence in the nineteenth century, two intellectual strains merged with an older, more universalist natural-law tradition to produce a distinctively Latin American discourse of rights. She traces its roots to the Spanish Dominicans — above all Bartolomé de Las Casas, the sixteenth-century bishop who condemned slavery and defended Native peoples on the basis of a natural right to liberty grounded in a single common humanity: “All the peoples of the world are humans,” Las Casas wrote, “and all the races of humankind are one.” Following Paolo Carozza and Brian Tierney, Glendon credits Las Casas and his fellow Dominicans with laying the groundwork for a doctrine of natural rights independent of religious revelation, drawn instead from human rationality and free will and from Aristotelian philosophy.
options: African slavery was a direct result of Spanish settlements in Florida.
Early native civilizations in Mexico introduced Spanish explorers to cattle ranching and wheat cultivation.
Christopher Columbus was not the first European to have explored North America.
Because of racial prejudice, Spanish explorers shunned intermarriage with native people.
items.explanation: Although many people assume Columbus to be the first European to explore North America, Scandinavians had previously explored areas in the northern part of this continent. The Spanish were not directly responsible for slavery, so rule out (A). Early Mexicans did not raise cattle or wheat, so rule out (B). And the Spanish did, in fact, intermarry extensively with native peoples throughout Mexico and South America, so rule out (D).

items.stem: The ideas represented in the excerpt above were most reflected in American policy in the 20th century through

options: Moral Imperialism
Cold War politics
the Good Neighbor Policy
free trade agreements like NAFTA
items.explanation: The excerpt mentions injustices and colonization attempts against people in Latin America, so we would want to try to eliminate examples of the United States doing that in the 20th century. Moral imperialism, while it has the word “moral” in the name, wasn’t exactly welcomed by most Latin American states under Wilson. In the Cold War, the United States intervened strongly against perceived communist threats in Latin America, but again, this wouldn’t fit the message of Las Casas. Free trade agreements have also come under strong criticism by people in Latin America (especially those of Indigenous descent); the best answer is (C), Roosevelt’s Good Neighbor Policy.

items.stem: The food cultivation system of the Native American groups referenced in the stimulus above is most analogous to which of the following North American indigenous food systems?

options: Buffalo hunting among the Lakota Sioux
Wolf domestication by the Algonquians
Mixed agriculture among the Iroquois
Seal hunting among the Inuit
items.explanation: The spread of maize cultivation from present-day Mexico northward into the American Southwest and beyond supported economic development in these areas and allowed tribes to remain in fixed communities. This is most similar to the fixed agricultural and fishing communities of the Iroquois. Buffalo and seal hunting would require some degree of migration, so rule out (A) and (D), while (B), wolf domestication, would not provide a steady supply of food.

items.stem: Proponents of the theological ideas that were criticized by Williams in the excerpt believed that freedom to practice religion should be extended to
items.stimulus: “I observe the great and wonderful mistake, both our own and our fathers, as to the civil powers of this world, acting in spiritual matters. I have read…the last will and testament of the Lord Jesus over many times, and yet I cannot find by one tittle of that testament that if He had been pleased to have accepted of a temporal crown and government that ever He would have put forth the least finger of temporal or civil power in the matters of His spiritual affairs and Kingdom. Hence must it lamentably be against the testimony of Christ Jesus for the civil state to impose upon the souls of the people a religion, a worship, a ministry, oaths (in religious and civil affairs), tithes, times, days, marryings, and buryings in holy ground….” Source: Roger Williams, The Hireling Ministry None of Christ’s, 1652
options: Puritans only
all Protestants only
all Christians only
all Jews and Christians only
items.explanation: Believing that theirs was the one true church, the Puritans saw no contradiction in denying others the same rights they had sought in England.

items.stem: An opponent of the ideas expressed by Williams would most likely have supported which of these political parties in the 1800s?
items.stimulus: “I observe the great and wonderful mistake, both our own and our fathers, as to the civil powers of this world, acting in spiritual matters. I have read…the last will and testament of the Lord Jesus over many times, and yet I cannot find by one tittle of that testament that if He had been pleased to have accepted of a temporal crown and government that ever He would have put forth the least finger of temporal or civil power in the matters of His spiritual affairs and Kingdom. Hence must it lamentably be against the testimony of Christ Jesus for the civil state to impose upon the souls of the people a religion, a worship, a ministry, oaths (in religious and civil affairs), tithes, times, days, marryings, and buryings in holy ground….” Source: Roger Williams, The Hireling Ministry None of Christ’s, 1652
options: The American (Know-Nothing) Party
The Free-Soil Party
The Democratic-Republican Party
The Populist (People’s) Party
items.explanation: First, figure out what Williams’ claim is: that the church and state should largely be separate, and that the government should not be imposing a particular religion on its citizens. In the 1800s, only one of the four major political parties was interested in imposing a specific kind of religious conformity: the Know-Nothing Party, which wanted students reading Protestant Bibles in school and strong restrictions on Catholic immigration into America. For that reason, (A) is the best answer.

items.stem: The group that Williams criticizes in the excerpt would have been most likely to settle which of these regions of the American colonies?

I have read…the last will and testament of the Lord Jesus over many times, and yet I cannot find by one tittle of that testament that if He had been pleased to have accepted of a temporal crown and government that ever He would have put forth the least finger of temporal or civil power in the matters of His spiritual affairs and Kingdom. options: The southern Colonies
The New England Colonies
The Middle Colonies
The Chesapeake Colonies
items.explanation: To answer this question, figure out what group Williams is referencing, which appears to be the Puritans. If that is the case, Puritans were known for primarily establishing the Plymouth and Massachusetts Bay colonies, which were in New England, so (B) is the best choice.

items.stem: A historian could use this source to show
items.stimulus: “I observe the great and wonderful mistake, both our own and our fathers, as to the civil powers of this world, acting in spiritual matters. I have read…the last will and testament of the Lord Jesus over many times, and yet I cannot find by one tittle of that testament that if He had been pleased to have accepted of a temporal crown and government that ever He would have put forth the least finger of temporal or civil power in the matters of His spiritual affairs and Kingdom. Hence must it lamentably be against the testimony of Christ Jesus for the civil state to impose upon the souls of the people a religion, a worship, a ministry, oaths (in religious and civil affairs), tithes, times, days, marryings, and buryings in holy ground….” Source: Roger Williams, The Hireling Ministry None of Christ’s, 1652
options: how American colonies treated political dissidents
the influence of Puritanism on the English Civil War
the effects of British salutary neglect
the roots of the Constitution’s First Amendment
items.explanation: While you might know that Williams was a dissident who was exiled from Massachusetts Bay, the source does not explain this, so you can eliminate (A). Puritans did strongly influence the English Civil War, which happened to be going on when this source was written, but is not being directly referenced here. Salutary neglect also was practiced by the British authorities, but that has little to do with the Puritan government. However, the First Amendment guarantees the right to religious freedom, so this source can clearly be read as a predecessor to that, so (D) is the best answer.

items.stem: Which of the following documents encouraged church membership in the Massachusetts Bay Colony?
items.stimulus: “I observe the great and wonderful mistake, both our own and our fathers, as to the civil powers of this world, acting in spiritual matters. I have read…the last will and testament of the Lord Jesus over many times, and yet I cannot find by one tittle of that testament that if He had been pleased to have accepted of a temporal crown and government that ever He would have put forth the least finger of temporal or civil power in the matters of His spiritual affairs and Kingdom. Hence must it lamentably be against the testimony of Christ Jesus for the civil state to impose upon the souls of the people a religion, a worship, a ministry, oaths (in religious and civil affairs), tithes, times, days, marryings, and buryings in holy ground….” Source: Roger Williams, The Hireling Ministry None of Christ’s, 1652
options: The Mayflower Compact
The Fundamental Orders
The Halfway Covenant
The Cambridge Agreement
items.explanation: The Halfway Covenant extended the privilege of baptism to all children of baptized people, not just those who had the personal experience of conversion. The Covenant was an attempt to bring more people into the Church and do away with some of the distinctions between the “elect” and all others.

items.stem: A major weakness of the national government referenced above was that it
items.stimulus: “Permit us, then, earnestly to recommend these articles to the immediate and dispassionate attention of the legislatures of the respective states. Let them be candidly reviewed under a sense of the difficulty of combining in one system the various sentiments and interests of a continent divided into so many sovereign and independent communities, under a conviction of the absolute necessity of uniting all our councils and all our strength, to maintain and defend our common liberties….” Source: Journals of the Continental Congress, 1777
options: created a too-powerful chief executive
did not include a mechanism for their own amendment
made it too difficult for the government to raise money through taxes and duties
denied the federal government the power to mediate disputes between states
items.explanation: Choice (A) is incorrect because the Articles did not create an executive, just a unicameral, legislature. Choice (B) is incorrect because the Articles could be amended, but only by unanimous approval of the states. Choice (D) is incorrect; the Articles gave the government the power to mediate such disputes, on appeal raised by the states.

items.stem: The most notable achievement of the United States under the form of government referenced in the source above was
items.stimulus: “Permit us, then, earnestly to recommend these articles to the immediate and dispassionate attention of the legislatures of the respective states. Let them be candidly reviewed under a sense of the difficulty of combining in one system the various sentiments and interests of a continent divided into so many sovereign and independent communities, under a conviction of the absolute necessity of uniting all our councils and all our strength, to maintain and defend our common liberties….” Source: Journals of the Continental Congress, 1777
options: the creation of a strong executive office to lead the national government
the empowerment of Congress to regulate commerce
the empowerment of Congress to collect taxes
the provision for land sales in the Northwest that would benefit the entire nation
items.explanation: The land sales in the Northwest were structured so that they would benefit the entire nation and gave newly created states equal status with the older states. None of the other choices were actually accomplished under the Articles of Confederation, which did not provide for a strong central government.

items.stem: Which of the following groups would have been most supportive of the excerpt above?
items.stimulus: “And it hath accordingly happened that an open resistance to the execution of the laws hath actually taken place in the town of Boston, and the neighbourhood thereof, within the said province: And whereas it is, under these circumstances, become absolutely necessary…that the said method of annually electing the counsellors or assistants of the said province should no longer be suffered to continue but that the appointment of the said counsellors or assistants should henceforth be put upon the like footing as is established in such other of his Majesty’s colonies or plantations in America, the governors whereof are appointed by his Majesty’s commission, under the great seal of Great Britain…so much of the charter, granted by their majesties King William and Queen Mary to the inhabitants of the said province of the Massachusetts Bay, in New England, and all and every clause…be revoked…and that the offices of all counsellors and assistants, elected and appointed in pursuance thereof, shall from thenceforth cease and determine: And that, the council, or court of assistants of the said province for the time being, shall be composed of such of the inhabitants or proprietors of lands within the same as shall be thereunto nominated and appointed by his Majesty…” Source: The Coercive Acts, 1774
options: A participant in the Boston Tea Party
A delegate to the Stamp Act Congress
A colonial tax collector
An elected member of a colonial legislature
items.explanation: The stimulus above is describing the Coercive Acts, which you might remember were passed in response to the Boston Tea Party in order to remove powers from Massachusetts’s legislature and bring the colonies to heel. Someone who participated in the event that brought this law on probably would not be a supporter of it, so you can eliminate (A). Delegates to the Stamp Act Congress were not friendly to heavy-handed British laws, so you can eliminate (B). Because this source alludes to stripping the colonial legislature of its power, an elected colonial representative wouldn’t like this either, eliminating (D). However, the colonists often targeted tax collectors in their protests of British laws, so (C) is the best bet.

items.stem: The law referenced above was meant to accomplish all of the following EXCEPT
items.stimulus: “And it hath accordingly happened that an open resistance to the execution of the laws hath actually taken place in the town of Boston, and the neighbourhood thereof, within the said province: And whereas it is, under these circumstances, become absolutely necessary…that the said method of annually electing the counsellors or assistants of the said province should no longer be suffered to continue but that the appointment of the said counsellors or assistants should henceforth be put upon the like footing as is established in such other of his Majesty’s colonies or plantations in America, the governors whereof are appointed by his Majesty’s commission, under the great seal of Great Britain…so much of the charter, granted by their majesties King William and Queen Mary to the inhabitants of the said province of the Massachusetts Bay, in New England, and all and every clause…be revoked…and that the offices of all counsellors and assistants, elected and appointed in pursuance thereof, shall from thenceforth cease and determine: And that, the council, or court of assistants of the said province for the time being, shall be composed of such of the inhabitants or proprietors of lands within the same as shall be thereunto nominated and appointed by his Majesty…” Source: The Coercive Acts, 1774
options: provide Britain with the ability to select governing officials in the Massachusetts Bay Colony
require the quartering of Britain’s officials and military in the homes of Massachusetts Bay residents
revoke the rule of governance outlined in the Massachusetts Bay Charter
punish the Massachusetts Bay Colony for the events of the Boston Tea Party
items.explanation: As described above, the Massachusetts Government Act aimed to seize control and punish the people of the Massachusetts Bay Colony for the “open resistance” that took place in Boston harbor, (D). As part of this act, the charter of 1691, which outlined the governance of the colony, was revoked, (C), and the election and governance of all government officials would be now decided by the monarchy, (A). This act had no direct impact on the decision to permit quartering of British soldiers, (B), which was made legal with the newly revised Quartering Act of 1774.

items.stem: Which of the following occurred in direct response to the policy referenced above?
items.stimulus: “And it hath accordingly happened that an open resistance to the execution of the laws hath actually taken place in the town of Boston, and the neighbourhood thereof, within the said province: And whereas it is, under these circumstances, become absolutely necessary…that the said method of annually electing the counsellors or assistants of the said province should no longer be suffered to continue but that the appointment of the said counsellors or assistants should henceforth be put upon the like footing as is established in such other of his Majesty’s colonies or plantations in America, the governors whereof are appointed by his Majesty’s commission, under the great seal of Great Britain…so much of the charter, granted by their majesties King William and Queen Mary to the inhabitants of the said province of the Massachusetts Bay, in New England, and all and every clause…be revoked…and that the offices of all counsellors and assistants, elected and appointed in pursuance thereof, shall from thenceforth cease and determine: And that, the council, or court of assistants of the said province for the time being, shall be composed of such of the inhabitants or proprietors of lands within the same as shall be thereunto nominated and appointed by his Majesty…” Source: The Coercive Acts, 1774
options: The convening of the First Continental Congress
The events of the Boston Massacre
The drafting of the Declaration of Independence
The writing of Letters From a Farmer in Pennsylvania by John Dickinson
items.explanation: While the Coercive Acts largely targeted Massachusetts Bay, the infringement on the rights and governance of the colony elevated concern throughout the colonies, which ultimately prompted the First Continental Congress to discuss grievances and a response. The Boston Massacre, (B), occurred several years prior (1770) to the Massachusetts Government Act. Although only two years away, a declaration for independence, (C), was not yet on the table, as the colonies felt that they might still be able to reconcile with the Crown through diplomacy. The Letters From a Farmer in Pennsylvania by John Dickinson, (D), was a series of essays written against the impacts of the earlier Townshend Acts.

items.stem: The author would be most supportive of which of the following claims?
options: Government is unnecessary, since personal conscience guides humanity.
A limited republican government is preferable to a monarchy.
Government is a necessary check against the corrupting influence of society.
Security is the only justification for government.
items.explanation: Since Paine describes government as a “ necessary evil,” (A) is too extreme. Choice (C) is wrong because Paine states that society is a “blessing.” The word “only” makes (D) too extreme.

items.stem: Which of the following “miseries” alluded to above were most condemned by Anti-Federalists of the Post-Revolutionary Era?
options: Organized response to Bacon’s Rebellion
Federal response to Shays’s Rebellion
Federal response to the Whiskey Rebellion
Federal response to Pontiac’s Rebellion
items.explanation: The key to this question is its reference to the Anti-Federalists. The Anti-Federalists were suspicious of centralized government power and were leery of Washington’s military response to the Whiskey Rebellion in 1794. The response to Shays’s Rebellion was weak; it would not have posed a perceived threat, so eliminate (B). Choices (A), Bacon’s Rebellion, and (D), Pontiac’s Rebellion, occurred prior to the Revolution, so these answers can be ruled out immediately.

items.stem: Which of the following is a claim invoked by the author above?
options: Colonists were destined to leave the British Empire because of the distance between the New World and England.
Women are biologically predestined to lives of child-rearing and domestic labor.
America’s expansion to the West Coast was inevitable and divinely sanctioned.
The abolition of slavery in the United States was certain to come about because slavery was immoral.
items.explanation: O’Sullivan makes reference to God and the tone of the passage is clear and confident, so (C) is the best choice. No mention is made of distances, so rule out (A). Neither women nor enslaved people are mentioned, so rule out (B) and (D), respectively.

items.stem: When O’Sullivan uses the phrase “nation of many nations,” he is most likely referring to
options: people of Indigenous origin
people living in American colonies overseas
people living in slavery
people migrating to the United States
items.explanation: O’Sullivan seems to speak positively of this “nation of many nations,” saying it is “destined to manifest to mankind the excellence of divine principles.” Indigenous people don’t really fit into that model for supporters of Manifest Destiny, so you can safely eliminate (A). America did not yet have a system of overseas colonies yet, eliminating (B). While slavery did exist at this time, it’s probably not what O’Sullivan had in mind when writing this. In the 1830s and 40s, however, there was a large wave of migration into the country from places like Ireland, so (D) is the best answer.

items.stem: All of the following from 1800 to 1848 helped reinforce the perspective expressed by O’Sullivan above EXCEPT
options: southern leaders' growing view of slavery as a 'positive good'
a sense of perfectionism that emerged out of religious movements
a wave of patriotism in the wake of conflicts with Great Britain
a new American literary tradition based on individualism
items.explanation: For this source, it is acknowledging that America is developing a distinctive national identity, so you want the answer choice that most challenges that. Choice (B) seems to fit O’Sullivan’s idea that America can manifest “the excellence of divine principles.” For (C), after the War of 1812, many Americans are newly enamored of what the flag represents, which goes with the source too. For (D), many authors like Edgar Allen Poe and Ralph Waldo Emerson helped create a uniquely American literary tradition based on individualism, so you should eliminate that answer. However, the idea of slavery as a positive good was particular to the South and doesn’t seem to go along with O’Sullivan’s idea of “owning no man master,” so (A) is the best choice.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a change in westward migration in the 1840s?
options: The number of pioneers headed for the Oregon Territory decreased while the number headed for California greatly increased.
The first great wave of migration ended, and the number of migrants remained extremely low until after the Civil War.
For the first time, pioneers began to settle areas west of the Mississippi River.
Large numbers of free Black people, unwelcome in the East, began to resettle in the West.
items.explanation: In January 1848, a carpenter discovered gold at Sutter’s Mill, California. Word spread quickly, and soon the Gold Rush was on. Western migrants continued to travel west on the Oregon Trail until they reached Fort Hall (in modern Idaho), but then they turned south on the California Trail and headed for where the gold was supposed to be. Most wound up disappointed, as only a very few found much gold. In seven years, California’s population grew from 15,000 to 300,000. One observer noted that, by 1849, the western section of the Oregon Trail (which led into the Oregon Territory) “bore no evidence of having been much traveled.”

items.stem: By what means did the United States take possession of the Oregon Territory?
options: The United States was granted the territory in a postwar treaty with France.
The United States bought it from the Native Americans who lived there.
U.S. settlers were the first to arrive in the region; they claimed it for their country.
Great Britain ceded it to the United States as part of a negotiated treaty.
items.explanation: The United States almost fought a war over the Oregon Territory, which consisted of present-day Oregon, Washington, and parts of Montana and Idaho. Originally, American expansionists and settlers demanded all the territory up to the 54°40′ boundary, and they were willing to fight the British (who held it as part of their Canadian territories) to get it. Contemporaneous conflicts near Mexico caused President Polk to reconsider war with Great Britain; he feared that two wars would spread forces dangerously thin, as well as damage his popularity with voters. Therefore, Polk decided to negotiate a settlement with the British—the United States accepted a boundary at the 49th parallel—and directed his military activities southward. The United States subsequently entered a war with Mexico, which netted them much of the territory that makes up the southwestern states.

items.stem: Which of the following represents a consequence of the ideology expressed by the author above between 1800 and 1865?
options: Debates over the expansion of slavery intensified.
New religious denominations such as Mormonism emerged.
Women began organizing more explicitly around political causes such as temperance and suffrage.
Politicians argued for increased tariffs to protect nascent American industry.
items.explanation: Since the ideology expressed above is Manifest Destiny, you need to find an example here that connects to that. While Mormonism did come out of this period (and is associated with Western expansion), that is more a product of the Second Great Awakening in New York, so eliminate it. Women organizing politically isn’t explicitly connected to expansion either, so eliminate (C). Lastly, the debate over the tariff had been happening since the days of Hamilton, removing (D). The intensifying debate over slavery is the most salient effect, so choose (A).

items.stem: The court case referenced in the source above upheld which of the following principles?
options: The existence of “separate but equal” facilities for people of different races was constitutional.
Corporations were entitled to the same protections guaranteed to individuals under the Fourteenth Amendment.
School prayer violated the principle of “separation of church and state.”
Congress had no right to regulate slavery in United States territories.
items.explanation: Dred Scott was an enslaved person whose owner had traveled with him into the free state of Illinois and also into the Wisconsin Territory, where slavery was prohibited. Scott declared himself a free man, and a series of court cases ruled variously for and against his claim. The case finally reached the Supreme Court in 1857. Taney’s ruling was remarkable in that it far exceeded the scope of the case. Taney could simply have ruled on the merits of the case; instead, he decided to establish a wide-ranging precedent. Enslaved people, he said, were property, and as such could be transported anywhere. Because enslaved people were not citizens, Taney further reasoned, they could not sue in federal court (thereby eliminating the possibility of the court reviewing any such cases in the future). Taney topped off his decision by stating that Congress could neither prevent settlers from transporting their enslaved people to western territories nor could it legislate slavery in those areas, thus nullifying the Missouri Compromise and rendering the concept of popular sovereignty unconstitutional. Taney’s decision is infamous for its lack of compassion for Scott and enslaved people, and it is significant in that it hastened the inevitable Civil War. Choice (A) describes Plessy v. Ferguson, (B) describes many Supreme Court cases of the 1890s, and (C) describes Engle v. Vitale . You should know the Plessy and Dred Scott decisions, but not Engle , by name.

items.stem: In what way did the actions of Abraham Lincoln in 1860 contradict Douglass’s sentiments in the excerpt above?
options: Lincoln promoted the freedom of settlers within territories to determine the slave status of their new state.
Lincoln passed the Homestead Act to give free land to all western settlers.
Lincoln favored the exclusion of slavery from any of the new territories.
Lincoln enacted the policy of giving newly freed enslaved people “forty acres and a mule.”
items.explanation: In the excerpt, Douglass asserts that slaveholders have an advantage because they control all aspects of government. He states that “the Federal Government…is pledged to support, defend, and propagate the crying curse of human bondage.” This may have been true in 1857, but Lincoln turned the tables in 1860 by running on a Free-Soil platform, thus opposing the institution of slavery. He did not promote popular sovereignty, so rule out (A). The Homestead Act is irrelevant to this question, so rule out (B). The enslaved people were not freed in 1860, so rule out (D).

items.stem: The excerpt from Frederick Douglass is most clearly an example of which of the following developments in the mid-19th century?
options: The gradual replacement of indentured servants with enslaved Africans
The preservation of African culture through cultural adaptation
Southern influence upon the federal government to defend the institution of slavery
The success of abolitionists to sway majority public opinion
items.explanation: Many white Americans in the South asserted their regional identity through pride in the institution of slavery, insisting that the federal government should defend that institution. Indentured servants had long been replaced by enslaved people before 1857, so rule out (A). Douglass does not appear to be “adapting,” so rule out (B). And, although Douglass was an abolitionist, he has not apparently swayed the opinion of Southerners, according to his own words, so rule out (D).

items.stem: Which of the following groups would be most likely to support the perspective of Frederick Douglass?
options: Southern Democrats in the 1880s
Western ranchers in the 1850s
Southern farmers in the 1830s
Northern Republicans in the 1860s
items.explanation: Northern Republicans were most prone to abolitionist sentiments in 1857. Southerners in general were more likely to defend or tolerate slavery, so rule out (A) and (C). Western ranchers, (B), were not known for having strong abolitionist views, although many were no doubt sympathetic to Douglass. Choice (D) is a better answer.

items.stem: Frederick Douglass was most influenced by which of the following social movements?
options: First Great Awakening
Second Great Awakening
Manifest Destiny
Popular Sovereignty
items.explanation: In the Northeast, the Second Great Awakening gave birth to numerous societies dedicated to the task of saving humanity from its own worst impulses. Much of the language of reform had a religious tone. For example, drinking and poverty were considered social evils. The religious and moral fervor that accompanied the Second Great Awakening also persuaded more and more Northerners that slavery was a great evil.

items.stem: Which of the following political movements most closely shared the goals outlined by the platform above?
items.stimulus: “We have witnessed for more than a quarter of a century the struggles of the two great political parties for power and plunder, while grievous wrongs have been inflicted upon the suffering people. We charge that the controlling influences dominating both these parties have permitted the existing dreadful conditions to develop without serious effort to prevent or restrain them. Neither do they now promise us any substantial reform. They have agreed together to ignore, in the coming campaign, every issue but one. They propose to drown the outcries of a plundered people with the uproar of a sham battle over the tariff, so that capitalists, corporations, national banks, rings, trusts, watered stock, the demonetization of silver and the oppressions of the usurers may all be lost sight of. They propose to sacrifice our homes, lives, and children on the altar of mammon; to destroy the multitude in order to secure corruption funds from the millionaires. “Assembled on the anniversary of the birthday of the nation, and filled with the spirit of the grand general and chief who established our independence, we seek to restore the government of the Republic to the hands of ‘the plain people,’ with which class it originated. We assert our purposes to be identical with the purposes of the National Constitution; to form a more perfect union and establish justice, insure domestic tranquility, provide for the common defence, promote the general welfare, and secure the blessings of liberty for ourselves and our posterity.” Source: Populist Party Platform, 1892
options: George McGovern, Democratic Party, 1972
Theodore Roosevelt, Progressive Party, 1912
Andrew Jackson, Democratic Party, 1829
H. Ross Perot, Reform Party, 1996
items.explanation: The excerpt specifically decries the “two great political parties” and asserts that “grievous wrongs have been inflicted upon the suffering people.” This is most similar to the third-party presidential candidate H. Ross Perot, who ran for office twice in the 1990s, lambasting both Democrats and Republicans in his bid for independent-minded voters. Choices (A), George McGovern, and (C), Andrew Jackson, were not critics of political parties, per se. Theodore Roosevelt is a close choice, since Progressives did adopt some Populist ideals, but he was not as much of an outlier as Perot. Choice (D) is the best choice.
